tur45-4: No. Despite the name, growing pains have nothing to do with growing and are not a sign of a serious illness. The cause is not known. They are more common in active children and after days with a lot of sport, and are also common in children with joint hypermobility (connective tissue laxity). In a 2022 review of 145 studies and 2 diagnostic systems, 93% of the studies using the term growing pains made no mention of growth in their definition.

tur45-7: Because a head tilt in babies can have other causes, a doctor and a children’s physiotherapist should assess your baby first. The American Physical Therapy Association’s guideline recommends referring a baby to their doctor and to a physiotherapist experienced with infants as soon as a head tilt or a preference for looking to one side is noticed.
tur45-8: With your baby on their back, gently hold the shoulder on the other side steady and slowly turn their head towards the affected side, so that their chin comes over the shoulder on the affected side.
tur45-9: With treatment, most babies regain full movement of their neck; the muscle stretches as it grows and is stretched. Without treatment, neck movement may stay permanently limited and surgery may be needed later. If there is no improvement within 3 months of physiotherapy, an orthopaedic assessment may be requested.
tur45-10: According to the American Physical Therapy Association’s guideline, treatment can end when your baby’s neck moves to within 5 degrees of the other side, there is no visible head tilt, your baby can do the movements expected for their age and moves equally to both sides, and you have learnt the exercises and what to watch for.
